note: 30-day practices keyed by group id from questions.json. The plan is assembled from the visitor's lowest-scoring groups (their development edges). These are practices, not remediation tickets.
framing: A thirty-day plan is short on purpose. Two or three practices, done, beat a roadmap nobody starts.

governance.label: Governance & Strategy
governance.week1: Write your security posture on one page: what you protect, what you have accepted, and who owns each. One page, no appendix.
governance.month: Put a standing fifteen-minute security item on the leadership meeting with three numbers you will report every time.

product.label: Product & Engineering Security
product.week1: Threat-model one feature currently in build — the next one to ship, not a hypothetical. One hour, with the engineers who are building it.
product.month: Turn what that session surfaced into the first two entries of a secure-development checklist the team actually uses.

devsecops.label: DevSecOps & Vulnerability Remediation
devsecops.week1: Measure one number honestly: median days from vulnerability disclosure to production fix, over the last quarter.
devsecops.month: Set a severity ranking and an SLA against that measured baseline — not against an aspirational one.

trust.label: Customer Trust & Compliance
trust.week1: Take the last enterprise security questionnaire you received and mark every answer that cost more than ten minutes to produce.
trust.month: Write the standing answers to those questions once, so the next questionnaire is assembly rather than authorship.

incident.label: Incident Readiness
incident.week1: Name the roles: who declares an incident, who talks to customers, who talks to engineering. Three names, written down.
incident.month: Run one ninety-minute tabletop on a realistic scenario. The output is the list of things that did not work.

balance.label: Balance
balance.week1: Before your next high-pressure security conversation, take sixty seconds to settle and decide the one thing you need the meeting to establish.
balance.month: Pick the one security commitment you have quietly let slip and close it — or formally let it go, out loud.

flexibility.label: Flexibility
flexibility.week1: Name one security approach you are carrying out of habit rather than need. Just name it this week.
flexibility.month: Retire it, or rebuild it around how the work is actually done now.

vitality.label: Vitality
vitality.week1: Notice where in the week your security attention actually runs out, and write down what precedes it.
vitality.month: Protect one recurring block of unfragmented time and defend it for four weeks. Note what changes.

heart.label: Heart
heart.week1: Ask one engineer what security costs them in an ordinary week. Ask, then stay quiet long enough to hear the second answer.
heart.month: Change one thing they named. Tell them you changed it and why.

voice.label: Voice
voice.week1: Rewrite your current top security risk in one sentence a non-technical director could repeat accurately.
voice.month: Use it in a real forum — board, leadership, all-hands — and notice which part gets misheard. Fix that part.

vision.label: Vision
vision.week1: Take thirty minutes with no agenda and no laptop, and write what a security programme that clearly enabled growth would look like here in a year.
vision.month: Turn that into three priorities with owners, and delete everything on your current list that does not serve them.

inspiration.label: Inspiration
inspiration.week1: Write down the security question you do not currently have an answer to and have been avoiding.
inspiration.month: Spend one hour a week on it, with no requirement to resolve it. Record what you notice.
